extracted.intended_audience: students, clinicians, and general readers interested in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes major psychoanalytic theories, core tenets, diagnostic/clinical indicators, therapeutic aims and metapsychological points of view used to evaluate mental functioning and psychopathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic tenets of psychoanalysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Core assumptions about development, drives, and treatment listed as numbered tenets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: (1) beside inherited constitution, development is determined by events in early childhood; (2) human behavior, experience, and cognition are largely determined by irrational drives; (3) those drives are largely unconscious; (4) attempts to bring those drives into awareness meet psychological resistance in the form of defense mechanisms; (5) conflicts between conscious and unconscious (repressed) material can result in mental disturbances such as neurosis, neurotic traits, anxiety, depression etc.; (6) liberation from effects of unconscious material is achieved through bringing this material into the conscious mind (via e.g. skilled guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freudian psychoanalytic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of classical Freudian psychoanalytic treatment and how it operates clinically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freudian psychoanalysis involves the analysand verbalizing thoughts (free associations, fantasies, dreams); the analyst induces/identifies unconscious conflicts causing symptoms and interprets them to create insight; the analyst confronts and clarifies pathological defenses, wishes and guilt; treatment hypothesizes how unconscious symbolic reactions produce symptoms and aims to bring unconscious material into consciousness for resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topographic theory (Freud)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metapsychological point of view dividing the mind into Conscious, Pre-conscious and Unconscious systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posits mental apparatus as process systems rather than brain anatomy; useful for describing how unacceptable wishes become unconscious; historically superseded in some places by Structural theory but remains a descriptive viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural theory (id, ego, superego)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model dividing the psyche into id (instinctual drives), ego (mediator operating on reality principle), and superego (self-observation and self-criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Id: present at birth, pleasure principle; Ego: develops to mediate id urges with external reality; Superego: reflective and judgemental faculties; ego and superego are partly conscious/partly unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomous ego functions (evaluation criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of ego functions considered 'autonomous' and evaluable in clinical assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions include: sensory perception, motor control, symbolic thought, logical thought, speech, abstraction, integration (synthesis), orientation, concentration, judgment about danger, reality testing, adaptive ability, executive decision-making, hygiene, and self-preservation. Deficits in these functions suggest psychoses or organic illness; some can be secondarily affected by unconscious conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ego strengths (clinical markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacities that indicate healthy ego functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ego strengths include capacities to control oral, sexual, and destructive impulses; to tolerate painful affects without 'falling apart'; and to prevent eruption into consciousness of bizarre symbolic fantasy. Presence/absence helps distinguish diagnostic categories and treatment focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six 'points of view' for evaluating unconscious processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical metapsychological frameworks for analyzing psychological phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six points of view are: 1. Topographic 2. Dynamic (theory of conflict) 3. Economic (theory of energy flow) 4. Structural 5. Genetic (origin/development of psychological functions) 6. Adaptational (relating psychological phenomena to the external world). These provide complementary lenses for evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object relations clinical indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Symptoms and capacities that signal disturbances in object relations theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical symptoms suggesting object relations problems include disturbances in capacity to feel warmth, empathy, trust, sense of security, identity stability, consistent emotional closeness, and stability in relationships with significant others. Developmental delays across life and difficulties with self/other internal representations are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern conflict theory therapeutic aim
rubrics_metrics.description: How modern conflict-theory psychoanalysis conceptualizes symptoms and the aim of therapy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Views emotional symptoms and character traits as complex solutions to mental conflict; dispenses with fixed id/ego/superego boundaries; therapy aims to change the balance of conflict by making less adaptive compromise formations conscious so more adaptive solutions can be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self psychology treatment focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles guiding treatment in self psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes development of a stable, integrated sense of self through empathic contacts with 'selfobjects' that provide mirroring, idealization, and twinship; treatment proceeds via 'transmuting internalizations' in which the patient internalizes selfobject functions provided by the therapist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lacanian psychoanalytic criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Core concepts and evaluative orientation of Lacanian analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrates structural linguistics and Hegelian philosophy; key concepts include the 'mirror stage', the 'Real', the 'Imaginary' and the 'Symbolic', and the claim that 'the unconscious is structured as a language'. Lacanian analysts advocate a return to Freud's complete works and use these constructs to analyze subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpersonal psychoanalysis emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical emphasis and evaluative focus of interpersonal psychoanalysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accents nuances of interpersonal interactions, how individuals protect themselves from anxiety via collusive interactions, and the relevance of actual developmental and present relationships (family, peers) to current functioning. Contrasts with primacy of intrapsychic forces in classical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive paradigm of psychotherapy (Langs)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the adaptive paradigm frames psychic conflict and model preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets psychic conflict in terms of conscious and unconscious adaptation to reality; tends to prefer a modified topographic model and emphasizes trauma (often death-related) as central; links psychoanalytic formulation with evolutionary biological principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational psychoanalysis therapeutic orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Relational approach to personality and therapy goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines interpersonal and intersubjective theory, emphasizing personality shaped by real and imagined relationships and how relational patterns are re-enacted in analyst–patient interactions. Promotes capacities like mentalization and addresses intergenerational transmission of attachment and trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersubjective psychoanalysis perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation lens emphasizing mutual influence between subjectivities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on how personality development and therapeutic process are influenced by the interrelationship between the patient's subjective perspective and that of others (including the analyst).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychopathology diagnostic distinctions (psychoanalytic view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychoanalytic criteria distinguishing psychoses, borderline conditions, and neurotic symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychoses: involve deficits in autonomous ego functions (integration, abstraction, reality testing), often impairing relationships. Borderline: deficits often in impulse/affect/fantasy control but reality testing more intact. Antisocial/psychopathy: lack of guilt and shame, chronic criminal behavior. Neurotic symptoms (panic, phobia, conversion, OCD, depression): typically caused by intrapsychic conflicts among wishes, guilt/shame, emotions and defenses rather than ego function deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childhood origins and oedipal formulation as etiological criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychoanalytic claims about childhood factors in the genesis of adult problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud held many adult problems trace to unresolved conflicts from certain childhood phases (e.g., the Oedipus complex in preschool years). The seduction theory (early view) posited infantile sexual excitations/trauma as basis for hysterical symptoms, but Freud revised some claims; psychoanalysis recognizes both effects of real abuse and the role of unconscious fantasies in development.
